However, the normative rule states that v0-v31 are architectural vector registers added to the ISA, meaning they should be accessible as source and destination registers across all vector instruction types (arithmetic, load/store, mask, etc.), not just as vs2 operands for floating-point move instructions.
gaps: No coverage of v0-v31 as vs1 source registers; No coverage of v0-v31 as vd destination registers; No coverage of v0-v31 used in vector load/store instructions; No coverage of v0-v31 used in vector integer/fixed-point instructions; No coverage of v0 used as mask register

spec_text: A vector context status field, VS, is added to mstatus[10:9] and shadowed in sstatus[10:9].  It is defined analogously to the floating-point context status field, FS.
coverage_desc_1: Coverpoint exercises the mstatus.VS field across all 4 states (Off/Initial/Clean/Dirty) with vector arithmetic instructions
explanation: The coverpoints test mstatus.VS across all 4 states with vector arithmetic instructions, which covers the VS field in mstatus[10:9]. However, the spec text also states VS is 'shadowed in sstatus[10:9]', meaning writes to mstatus.VS should be visible in sstatus.VS and vice versa. The coverpoints named 'cp_vsstatus_vs_off' appear to test vsstatus (the hypervisor extension register), not sstatus. Additionally, the spec says VS is 'defined analogously to the floating-point context status field, FS', implying the same state transition semantics (Initial→Clean→Dirty based on vector register access) should be verified, which may not be fully covered by just exercising all 4 states.
gaps: sstatus[10:9] shadowing of mstatus.VS is not explicitly covered - coverpoints reference vsstatus not sstatus; Analogous behavior to FS state transitions (e.g., vector access sets VS to Dirty, context save/restore transitions) is not explicitly tested

spec_text: When mstatus.VS is set to Initial or Clean, executing any instruction that changes vector state, including the vector CSRs, will change mstatus.VS to Dirty. Implementations may also change mstatus.VS from Initial or Clean to Dirty at any time, even when there is no change in vector state.
coverage_desc_1: Coverpoint cycles through mstatus.VS values 0-3 including Initial and Clean states, partially covering the dirty transition when vector instructions execute with those states
coverage_desc_2: The coverpoint tests an instruction that changes vector state (a vector floating-point move), which should transition mstatus.VS from Initial or Clean to Dirty, partially covering this rule.
coverage_desc_3: The coverpoint starts with mstatus.VS clear and executes a vector instruction that changes vector state, which should transition mstatus.VS to Dirty per this rule.
explanation: The coverpoints test mstatus.VS transitions to Dirty when vector instructions execute, covering the main behavior. However, there are gaps in coverage.
gaps: No coverpoint explicitly tests the transition from both Initial (01) AND Clean (10) states separately to Dirty (11) - the coverpoints mention 'Initial or Clean' but don't clearly verify both starting states independently; No coverpoint tests that changes to vector CSRs (e.g., vtype, vl via vsetvli) also trigger the VS transition to Dirty, only vector register-modifying instructions are tested; The rule applies to mstatus.VS but in virtualized environments also sstatus.VS/vsstatus.VS - coverage of sstatus.VS dirty transitions from Initial/Clean is not explicitly addressed; No coverpoint tests the implementation-permitted behavior where VS may change from Initial/Clean to Dirty even without vector state changes (though this is optional behavior, testing it confirms compliance)

spec_text: When V=1 and neither vsstatus.VS nor mstatus.VS is set to Off, executing any instruction that changes vector state, including the vector CSRs, will change both mstatus.VS and vsstatus.VS to Dirty.

spec_text: Implementations must provide fractional LMUL settings that allow the narrowest supported type to occupy a fraction of a vector register corresponding to the ratio of the narrowest supported type’s width to that of the largest supported type’s width. For standard vector extensions with ELEN=32, fractional LMULs of 1/2 and 1/4 must be supported.  For standard vector extensions with ELEN=64, fractional LMULs of 1/2, 1/4, and 1/8 must be supported.

coverage_desc_3: For widening instructions (emul2 variant with vwredsum.vs, vwredsumu.vs) where vd has EEW=2*SEW and vs1 has EEW=SEW, cmp_vd_vs1 forces overlap with different EEW, which must be treated as mask- and tail-agnostic regardless of vta/vma settings.
coverage_desc_4: When vs3 and vs2 overlap and have different EEW (data EEW=SEW vs index EEW encoded in instruction), the instruction should be mask- and tail-agnostic regardless of vta/vma settings.
coverage_desc_5: For widening variants (fwv, fwred) where source and destination may overlap with different EEW, cr_vs2_vs1_edges exercises register combinations that trigger the agnostic override behavior on overlap.

The normative rule applies broadly to any source-destination overlap with different EEW, which includes widening operations (vd overlaps vs2 where vd has larger EEW), other LMUL settings, and potentially vd overlapping vs1 as well.
gaps: Missing widening case where vd overlaps source with different EEW; Missing other LMUL settings beyond LMUL=4; Missing vd overlap with vs1 when EEW differs; Missing verification that both mask-agnostic and tail-agnostic behavior are enforced regardless of vta/vma bit settings

spec_text: The largest vector register group used by an instruction can not be greater than 8 vector registers (i.e., EMUL≤8), and if a vector instruction would require greater than 8 vector registers in a group, the instruction encoding is reserved.  For example, a widening operation that produces a widened vector register group result when LMUL=8 is reserved as this would imply a result EMUL=16.
coverage_desc_1: The coverpoint directly tests the EMUL≤8 reservation rule by using LMUL=8 with a widening reduction, which would normally imply EMUL=16 and be reserved, but verifies the exception for reduction scalar destinations.
coverage_desc_2: Testing LMUL=4 with widening operations implies EMUL=8 for the destination, and the coverpoint explicitly excludes LMUL=8 because it would require EMUL=16 which is reserved per this rule.
coverage_desc_3: With LMUL=8 for vf8 operations, the destination EMUL=8 which is the maximum allowed, directly relevant to this constraint
coverage_desc_4: Directly tests that widening instructions with LMUL=8 (implying EMUL=16 for the destination) are reserved and cause a trap, which is exactly what this rule specifies.
coverage_desc_5: Directly tests that EMUL>8 is reserved by setting LMUL=8 with narrowing instructions (implying EMUL=16 for the source operand), confirming the instruction traps.
coverage_desc_6: Coverpoint directly tests that EMUL>8 (EMUL=16) is a reserved encoding by setting lmul=8 and sew=8 for vrgatherei16, expecting a trap
coverage_desc_7: Tests that EMUL=1/16 (less than minimum allowed) for vs1 indices is reserved, as the instruction encoding requires EMUL to be at least 1/8
coverage_desc_8: Coverpoint verifies the general rule that vector register groups larger than 8 are reserved, by producing EMUL=16 which exceeds the maximum
coverage_desc_9: Testing LMUL=mf8 with vzext.vf4 produces EMUL=1/32 which is below minimum legal LMUL, partially covering the reserved EMUL constraint
coverage_desc_10: Some test cases produce source EMUL below the minimum legal fractional LMUL (1/8), which is a reserved encoding per this rule
coverage_desc_11: Coverpoint tests that EMUL>8 is reserved by triggering a trap when index EMUL exceeds 8, directly exercising the constraint that vector register groups cannot exceed 8 registers.
coverage_desc_12: Tests the general EMUL out-of-range reservation rule by exercising the EMUL < 1/8 case for indexed load/store index operands
explanation: The coverpoint only tests one specific scenario: widening reductions with LMUL=8 where EMUL would be 16. However, the normative rule applies broadly to ANY vector instruction where the largest vector register group would exceed 8, not just widening reductions. The coverpoint also focuses on the exception case (reduction scalar destinations) rather than verifying that non-exception cases are properly treated as reserved.
gaps: No coverage for non-widening instructions where EMUL>8 would be reserved; No coverage for widening non-reduction instructions (e.g., widening arithmetic like vwadd) with LMUL=8 being treated as reserved; No coverage for other LMUL/SEW combinations that could produce EMUL>8 beyond just LMUL=8 widening; The existing coverpoint tests an exception to the rule rather than the rule itself - need coverage that reserved encodings are actually treated as reserved

spec_text: Widened scalar values, e.g., input and output to a widening reduction operation, are held in the first element of a vector register and have EMUL=1.
coverage_desc_1: The coverpoint tests that widened scalar values in widening reduction operations have EMUL=1 (not EMUL=2*LMUL), confirming LMUL=8 does not cause an illegal instruction.
coverage_desc_2: The emul2 variant for widening reductions (vwredsum.vs, vwredsumu.vs) exercises vs1 as the double-width scalar accumulator with EMUL=1, partially covering the scalar EMUL rule.
coverage_desc_3: cmp_vd_vs1 with emul2 variant for widening reductions (vwredsum.vs, vwredsumu.vs) tests vd=vs1 where vs1 is a widened scalar with EMUL=1, exercising the rule that widened scalar values have EMUL=1 regardless of LMUL.
coverage_desc_4: cp_vs1_edges emul2/wred variant tests widened scalar values in vs1 for widening reductions, where the scalar has EMUL=1 per the spec.
coverage_desc_5: The wred variant is used by widening reduction instructions (vwredsum.vs, vwredsumu.vs) where the scalar operand in vs1 is double-width with EMUL=1, testing edge values for widened scalar inputs.

While this verifies that widened scalar values use EMUL=1 at the extreme LMUL setting, it doesn't test other LMUL values or verify the scalar is actually held in the first element of the vector register.
gaps: No coverage for LMUL values other than 8 (e.g., LMUL=1,2,4 where EMUL would be 2,4,8); No verification that the widened scalar value is held in the first element of the vector register; No coverage for both input and output scalar operands (vs1 and vd) being correctly treated with EMUL=1

spec_text: Element operations that are masked off (inactive) never generate exceptions. ||| The destination vector register elements corresponding to masked-off elements are handled with either a mask-undisturbed or mask-agnostic policy depending on the setting of the vma bit in vtype ||| Where available, masking is encoded in a single-bit vm field in the  instruction (inst[25]).
coverage_desc_1: Tests that masked-off (inactive) element operations never generate exceptions, using vm[0]=1 with vl=1 to make element 0 inactive and confirming no FP exception is raised
coverage_desc_2: Coverpoint directly tests the spec rule that masked-off element operations never generate exceptions, using vm=1 and v0=1 to mask the active element
coverage_desc_3: The coverpoint uses vm=1 (masked) with v0=2 to mask off elements, and verifies that masked-off inactive elements never generate exceptions
coverage_desc_4: By testing vm corners, the coverpoint exercises masked-off element behavior and the vm field encoding that controls execution masking for the vfirst instruction.
coverage_desc_5: cp_masking_edges directly tests masking behavior: vm=1 enables masking, v0 edge patterns create various active/inactive element combinations, and vma=random exercises both undisturbed and agnostic policies for masked-off elements.

However, there is no coverpoint that tests the second sentence: that destination elements corresponding to masked-off elements are handled with either mask-undisturbed or mask-agnostic policy depending on the vma bit in vtype.
gaps: No coverpoint tests that masked-off destination elements follow mask-undisturbed policy when vma=0; No coverpoint tests that masked-off destination elements follow mask-agnostic policy when vma=1

spec_text: The mask value used to control execution of a masked vector instruction is always supplied by vector register v0.
coverage_desc_1: The coverpoint uses v0 as both mask source and data source, directly exercising the rule that v0 always supplies the mask value for masked instructions.
coverage_desc_2: Testing vm corners implicitly exercises that the mask value controlling masked execution comes from v0, as vfirst uses v0 for masking when vm=0.
coverage_desc_3: Relies on the fact that v0 is always the mask register for masked instructions, which is why vd=v0 creates the overlap conflict
coverage_desc_4: Relies on v0 being the mask register to create the overlap condition between vd and the mask source
coverage_desc_5: cp_masking_edges sets v0 to specific edge-case patterns (all 1s, all 0s, random, VLMAX-1 ones, VLMAX/2+1 ones) with vm=1, directly exercising that v0 supplies the mask value for masked instructions.
explanation: The normative rule states that v0 always supplies the mask value for masked vector instructions. cp_custom_masked_vs*_v0 directly tests this by using v0 as both mask source and data source in masked instructions, confirming v0 is the mask register. cp_vs2_vm_corners tests the vm field corners, exercising that when vm=0 (masked), v0 supplies the mask. Together these coverpoints verify that masked execution always uses v0 as the mask source.

spec_text: The destination vector register group for a masked vector instruction cannot overlap the source mask register (v0), unless the destination vector register is being written with a mask value (e.g., compares) or the scalar result of a reduction.  These instruction encodings are reserved.
coverage_desc_1: The coverpoint ensures vd!=v0 to avoid the reserved encoding where destination overlaps the mask register v0, verifying compliance with this constraint.
coverage_desc_2: Directly tests the exception to the overlap restriction: mask arithmetic operations write mask values to v0, which is explicitly allowed even when v0 is the mask register, confirming these encodings are not treated as reserved
coverage_desc_3: Directly tests that vd=v0 is reserved for a masked vector instruction, which is exactly what this rule specifies - destination vector register group cannot overlap source mask register v0
coverage_desc_4: Directly tests that vd=v0 with masking enabled and LMUL>1 is reserved, confirming the destination register group overlaps the source mask register v0 and traps
coverage_desc_5: Coverpoint tests that destination vd=v0 overlapping mask register v0 in a masked instruction is reserved
coverage_desc_6: cp_vd with nv0 variant for vmerge.vvm/vxm/vim excludes v0 from destinations, partially covering the rule that masked instruction destinations cannot overlap the source mask register v0.
coverage_desc_7: cmp_vd_vs1 with nv0 variant for vadc.vvm, vsbc.vvm, and vmerge.vvm avoids v0 for vd, partially covering the rule that the destination register group for masked instructions cannot overlap the v0 mask register.
coverage_desc_8: The nv0 variant for vadc.vvm, vsbc.vvm, vmadc.vvm, vmsbc.vvm, and vmerge.vvm excludes v0 from vs1/vs2 choices, ensuring these implicitly masked instructions don't alias their source operands with the implicit mask register v0.
coverage_desc_9: The nv0 variant for vmerge.vvm excludes v0 from vd=vs1=vs2, ensuring the destination does not overlap the implicit mask register v0, which would be a reserved encoding for masked instructions.
coverage_desc_10: The nv0 variant used by vfmerge.vfm excludes v0 from vd/vs2 choices, acknowledging that the destination register group cannot overlap v0 which serves as the implicit mask source for merge instructions.
coverage_desc_11: Edge values include v0 for both vs2 and vs1; when combined with masked instructions, this tests the constraint that destination cannot overlap mask register v0.
explanation: The coverpoints test the general case (vd!=v0 for masked instructions) and one exception (mask arithmetic writing to v0 while masked). However, the rule also explicitly allows reductions to write scalar results to v0 even when masked, which is not covered by any listed coverpoint.
gaps: Missing coverpoint for reduction instructions writing scalar result to v0 while masked (the reduction exception to the overlap restriction)

spec_text: When vstart ≥ vl, there are no body elements, and no elements are updated in any destination vector register group, including that no tail elements are updated with agnostic values.
coverage_desc_1: The coverpoint implicitly tests the exception to this rule: for whole register loads/stores, the usual 'no elements written if vstart >= vl' property does NOT apply, and instead evl is used. The coverpoint verifies this distinction.
coverage_desc_2: Coverpoint explicitly tests with vstart >= vl to verify trapping behavior even when there are no body elements to process.
coverage_desc_3: Coverpoint explicitly tests the vstart >= vl condition to verify trapping behavior even when there are no body elements
coverage_desc_4: cp_vl_0 sets vl=0 with vstart=0, so vstart >= vl, exercising the rule that no body elements exist and no elements are updated in any destination vector register group.
explanation: The coverpoint only tests the exception case for whole register loads/stores where vstart >= vl does NOT prevent element updates. It does not test the main rule itself: that for normal (non-whole-register) vector operations, when vstart >= vl, no body elements are updated and no tail elements are updated with agnostic values in the destination vector register group.
gaps: No coverpoint tests the primary behavior: that normal vector operations produce no element updates (body or tail) when vstart >= vl; No coverpoint verifies that tail elements are specifically not updated with agnostic values when vstart >= vl

spec_text: Instructions that write an x register or f register do so even when vstart ≥ vl, including when vl=0.
coverage_desc_1: Directly tests that f-register writing instructions execute even when vstart ≥ vl including vl=0, which is exactly what this rule specifies.
coverage_desc_2: Directly tests that instructions writing an x or f register execute even when vstart >= vl (with vl=0, vstart=0), matching the rule's specification exactly.

coverage_desc_4: cp_vl_0 applies to instructions like vmv.x.s, vcpop.m, vfirst.m that write x/f registers; these must still write even when vl=0, exercising this independence rule.
explanation: The rule states that instructions writing an x register or f register do so even when vstart >= vl, including when vl=0. cp_custom_f_freg_write_vl0 covers the f-register writing case when vstart >= vl including vl=0. cp_custom_gprWriting_vstart_eq_vl covers the x-register (and f-register) writing case when vstart >= vl with vl=0/vstart=0. Together they cover both x-register and f-register writing under the specified conditions.

spec_text: The prestart elements do not raise exceptions and do not update the destination vector register.
coverage_desc_1: The coverpoint sets vstart=1 so element 0 is a prestart element, and verifies that prestart elements do not raise exceptions
explanation: The coverpoint tests that prestart elements do not raise exceptions by setting vstart=1, which covers the 'do not raise exceptions' aspect. However, the normative rule also states that prestart elements 'do not update the destination vector register', and no coverpoint verifies that the destination register remains unchanged for prestart elements.
gaps: No coverpoint verifies that prestart elements do not update the destination vector register

spec_text: The inactive elements do not raise exceptions and do not update any destination vector register group unless masked agnostic is specified (vtype.vma=1), in which case inactive elements may be overwritten with 1s.
coverage_desc_1: Tests that inactive elements do not raise exceptions, specifically that a masked-off element performing vfrsqrt7(0) does not trigger an FP exception flag update
coverage_desc_2: Coverpoint verifies that masked-off (inactive) elements do not raise exceptions by masking the only active element and loading from address 0 which would otherwise trap
coverage_desc_3: With v0=2 masking, element 1 (the only body element given vstart=1, vl=2) is inactive, and the coverpoint verifies it does not raise exceptions
coverage_desc_4: Tests behavior of inactive (masked-off) elements in a reduction, verifying they are excluded from the operation while the scalar still participates
coverage_desc_5: cp_masking_edges v0 patterns (all 0s, VLMAX-1 ones, VLMAX/2+1 ones) create inactive elements that must not raise exceptions and must follow vma policy for destination updates.
explanation: The coverpoints thoroughly test the 'inactive elements do not raise exceptions' aspect across multiple scenarios (FP exceptions, load/store traps, masked reductions). However, the second clause of the rule — that inactive elements 'do not update any destination vector register group' — is not directly tested by any coverpoint. Additionally, the masked-agnostic exception ('unless vtype.vma=1, in which case inactive elements may be overwritten with 1s') is not covered by any of the listed coverpoints.
gaps: No coverpoint verifies that inactive elements do not update the destination vector register group (i.e., destination elements remain unchanged when vma=0); No coverpoint tests the masked-agnostic (vma=1) behavior where inactive elements may be overwritten with 1s

spec_text: The tail elements do not raise exceptions, and do not update any destination vector register group unless tail agnostic is specified (vtype.vta=1), in which case tail elements may be overwritten with 1s, or with the result of the instruction in the case of mask-producing instructions except for mask loads.  When LMUL < 1, the tail includes the elements past VLMAX that are held in the same vector register.
coverage_desc_1: Coverpoint uses LMUL=2 with vl=1 to ensure tail elements exist, verifying they do not raise exceptions when the instruction accesses an invalid address
coverage_desc_2: This rule states tail elements 'may be overwritten with the result of the instruction in the case of mask-producing instructions', which is exactly what the coverpoint tests by checking mask tail values against computed results

coverage_desc_4: cp_masking_edges sets vta=0 (undisturbed) with vl=VLMAX, testing that tail elements are not updated when tail-undisturbed is specified.
explanation: The coverpoints address tail elements not raising exceptions (cp_custom_maskLS_tail_no_exception) and mask-producing instructions potentially overwriting tail with results (cp_vs2_vs1_mask_corners), but several aspects of the rule are not covered.
gaps: No coverpoint tests that tail elements do not update destination register group when vta=0 (tail undisturbed policy); No coverpoint tests that tail elements may be overwritten with 1s when vta=1 for non-mask-producing instructions; No coverpoint tests the LMUL < 1 case where tail includes elements past VLMAX held in the same vector register; No coverpoint tests the exception for mask loads (mask loads should not overwrite tail with results even for mask-producing behavior)

spec_text: The vset{i}vl{i} instructions set the vtype and vl CSRs based on their arguments, and write the new value of vl into rd.

coverage_desc_2: The coverpoint passes vtype values through rs2 register for vsetvl, testing that all XLEN bits of rs2 are read as the new vtype encoding.

spec_text: If the vtype value is not supported by the implementation, then the vill bit is set in vtype, the remaining bits in vtype are set to zero ||| A vtype value with vill set is treated as an unsupported configuration. ||| Implementations must consider all bits of the vtype value to determine if the configuration is supported.  An unsupported value in any location within the vtype value must result in vill being set.
coverage_desc_1: The coverpoint requires setting vill=1 in vtype as a precondition, testing the state where vill is set
coverage_desc_2: Setting SEW=8 for FP operations may result in an unsupported vtype configuration causing vill to be set, which the coverpoint partially exercises.
coverage_desc_3: Coverpoint verifies that unsupported vtype values (reserved vsew encodings) cause vill to be set, directly testing that an unsupported value in the vtype field results in vill being set.

It does not test the mechanism of setting vill itself - i.e., configuring vtype with an unsupported value and verifying that vill gets set and remaining bits are zeroed. The rule requires testing that unsupported vtype configurations cause vill to be set, not just that instructions work correctly when vill is already set.
gaps: No test that an unsupported vtype value causes vill to be set; No test that remaining vtype bits are zeroed when vill is set; No test that all bits of vtype are considered when determining support (e.g., reserved bits, unsupported SEW/LMUL combinations)

spec_text: When rs1 is not x0, the AVL is an unsigned integer held in the x register specified by rs1, and the new vl value is also written to the x register specified by rd. ||| When rs1=x0 but rd≠x0, the maximum unsigned integer value (~0) is used as the AVL, and the resulting VLMAX is written to vl and also to the x register specified by rd. ||| When rs1=x0 and rd=x0, the instructions operate as if the current vector length in vl is used as the AVL, and the resulting value is written to vl, but not to a destination register.  This form can only be used when VLMAX and hence vl is not actually changed by the new SEW/LMUL ratio.

spec_text: The vset{i}vl{i} instructions first set VLMAX according to their vtype argument, then set vl obeying the following constraints: ||| vl = AVL if AVL ≤ VLMAX ceil(AVL / 2) ≤ vl ≤ VLMAX if AVL < (2 * VLMAX) vl = VLMAX if AVL ≥ (2 * VLMAX) Deterministic on any given implementation for same input AVL and VLMAX values These specific properties follow from the prior rules:  vl = 0 if  AVL = 0 vl > 0 if AVL > 0 vl ≤ VLMAX vl ≤ AVL a value read from vl when used as the AVL argument to vset{i}vl{i} results in the same value in vl, provided the resultant VLMAX equals the value of VLMAX at the time that vl was read
coverage_desc_1: cp_vl_0 requires setting vl=0 via vsetvl with AVL=0, exercising the property 'vl = 0 if AVL = 0'.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: All vector loads and stores may generate and accept a non-zero vstart value.
coverage_desc_1: An address fault on a vector load/store generates a non-zero vstart value corresponding to the faulting element, partially covering the vstart acceptance requirement.
coverage_desc_2: The coverpoint tests vector loads with non-zero vstart=1, verifying they accept and operate correctly with non-zero vstart values
explanation: The rule states all vector loads AND stores may generate and accept non-zero vstart. cp_exceptionsv_address_fault covers generation of non-zero vstart for both loads and stores via address faults. cp_custom_maskLS_prestart_no_exception covers acceptance of non-zero vstart for vector loads. However, there is no coverpoint explicitly testing that vector stores accept and operate correctly with non-zero vstart values.
gaps: No coverpoint tests vector stores accepting and operating correctly with a non-zero vstart value

spec_text: Vector load/store base registers and strides are taken from the GPR x registers.
coverage_desc_1: cp_rs1 exercises all GPR x registers as rs1 for vector load/store instructions, partially verifying that base registers are taken from the GPR x registers.
coverage_desc_2: cp_rs2 exercises all 32 GPR x registers (rs2=x0-x31) as the stride source for vector load/store instructions, partially covering the rule that strides are taken from GPR x registers.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: The base effective address for all vector accesses is given by the contents of the x register named in rs1.
coverage_desc_1: The coverpoint sets rs1=0 as the base effective address to create a scenario where element 0 would fault, testing base address behavior
coverage_desc_2: The coverpoint loads a base address into rs1 and verifies that indexed operations use this as the base effective address to which the zero-extended offset is added.
coverage_desc_3: cp_rs1 exercises all 32 scalar x registers (rs1=0-31) including for vector load/store instructions, covering that the base effective address is given by the contents of the x register named in rs1.
explanation: The coverpoints test base address usage in specific scenarios (rs1=0 for fault testing, and rs1 as base for indexed operations), but they don't comprehensively test that the base effective address is derived from the rs1 register contents across all vector access types (unit-stride, strided, indexed) and with varied non-zero base addresses.
gaps: No coverage of base address from rs1 for unit-stride vector loads/stores with non-zero addresses; No coverage of base address from rs1 for strided vector loads/stores; No coverage verifying different rs1 register choices (not just specific registers) provide the base address; No coverage of base address interaction with different vector memory access widths beyond SEW8/SEW16

spec_text: Vector unit-stride operations access elements stored contiguously in memory starting from the base effective address.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: Vector constant-stride operations access the first memory element at the base effective address, and then access subsequent elements at address increments given by the byte offset contained in the x register specified by rs2.
coverage_desc_1: cp_rs2 exercises all 32 GPR x registers as the rs2 stride operand for constant-stride load/store instructions (vlse8.v, vlse16.v, etc.), partially covering the rule that subsequent elements are accessed at byte offsets from the x register specified by rs2.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: Vector memory unit-stride and constant-stride operations directly encode EEW of the data to be transferred statically in the instruction to reduce the number of vtype changes when accessing memory in a mixed-width routine.
coverage_desc_1: Tests EEW encoding behavior for unit-stride and constant-stride operations, verifying unsupported widths raise exceptions
explanation: The coverpoint only tests the exception/trap behavior when unsupported EEW widths are used. The normative rule describes that unit-stride and constant-stride operations directly encode EEW in the instruction to reduce vtype changes for mixed-width routines. Testing exceptions for unsupported widths is one aspect, but the rule's core statement about EEW being statically encoded in the instruction is not directly tested.
gaps: No coverpoint verifying that supported EEW encodings (8, 16, 32, 64) correctly transfer data at the specified element width for unit-stride operations; No coverpoint verifying that supported EEW encodings correctly transfer data at the specified element width for constant-stride operations; No coverpoint testing mixed-width memory access routines where different EEW values are used without changing vtype

spec_text: For loads, the vd register will hold the first field loaded from the segment.  For stores, the vs3 register is read to provide the first field to be stored to each segment.
coverage_desc_1: cp_vs3 directly tests the vs3 source register for segment store instructions (vsseg*), covering the rule that vs3 provides the first field to be stored to each segment.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: Support for misaligned vector memory accesses is independent of an implementation’s support for misaligned scalar memory accesses.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: Vector misaligned memory accesses follow the same rules for atomicity as scalar misaligned memory accesses.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: However, even for the ordered form, accesses to the fields within an individual segment are not ordered with respect to each other.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: If element 0 raises an exception, vl is not modified, and the trap is taken.  If an element > 0 raises an exception, the corresponding trap is not taken, and the vector length vl is reduced to the index of the element that would have raised an exception.
coverage_desc_1: Tests that when element 0 raises an exception, the trap is taken, directly covering the first clause of this rule.
coverage_desc_2: Coverpoint directly tests that when element > 0 raises an exception, the trap is not taken and vl is reduced to the index of that element
explanation: The rule has two clauses: (1) element 0 exception causes trap taken and vl not modified, (2) element > 0 exception causes trap not taken and vl reduced to that element index. cp_exceptionsv_ffLS_first_elm_trap covers the trap-taken aspect of clause 1, and cp_custom_ffLS_update_vl covers clause 2 (trap not taken, vl reduced). However, clause 1 also explicitly states 'vl is not modified' when element 0 raises an exception, and no coverpoint verifies that vl remains unchanged in that scenario.
gaps: No coverpoint verifies that vl is not modified when element 0 raises an exception

spec_text: Vector indexed operations add the contents of each element of the vector offset operand specified by vs2 to the base effective address to give the effective address of each element.  The data vector register group has EEW=SEW, EMUL=LMUL, while the offset vector register group has EEW encoded in the instruction and EMUL=(EEW/SEW)*LMUL.
coverage_desc_1: The coverpoint exercises indexed load operations by adding vector offset elements (vs2) to the base effective address (rs1), verifying the correct effective address computation with zero-extended offsets.
coverage_desc_2: The coverpoint exercises vector indexed operations by adding vs2 element contents to the base effective address, verifying the address computation works correctly after truncation.
coverage_desc_3: Coverpoint exercises indexed load/store operations where the offset vector register group EMUL=(EEW/SEW)*LMUL exceeds the allowed range, testing the EMUL calculation for indexed operations.
coverage_desc_4: Exercises indexed load/store operations where the offset vector register group EMUL=(EEW/SEW)*LMUL falls below 1/8
coverage_desc_5: cp_vs2_edges with ls variant tests edge offset values in vs2 elements that are added to the base address for indexed load/store operations, directly exercising the indexed addressing mechanism.
coverage_desc_6: Testing vs3==vs2 for vsuxei* instructions exercises the indexed store operation where the same register supplies both the store data and the byte-address offsets, verifying correct operand handling.
explanation: The coverpoints test zero-extended offsets (for EEW > SEW cases where SEW is 8 or 16) and truncated offsets (for EEW < SEW cases), covering the address computation aspect. However, they miss coverage of the data vector register group having EEW=SEW and EMUL=LMUL, and the offset vector register group having EMUL=(EEW/SEW)*LMUL. The rule also states this applies to each element, but there is no coverpoint verifying that all elements are independently addressed. Additionally, store indexed operations are not explicitly mentioned in the coverpoint descriptions (only 'load operations' are referenced).
gaps: No coverage of data vector register group EEW=SEW, EMUL=LMUL relationship; No coverage of offset vector register group EMUL=(EEW/SEW)*LMUL relationship; Store indexed operations not explicitly covered (coverpoints only mention load operations); No per-element verification that each element independently computes its effective address

spec_text: Indexed operations use the explicit EEW encoding in the instruction to set the size of the indices used, and use SEW/LMUL to specify the data width.
coverage_desc_1: Indexed operations use explicit EEW encoding for index size - coverpoint tests these for unsupported EEW raising exceptions
coverage_desc_2: cp_vs2_edges is exercised across vluxei8/16/32/64 and similar instructions, testing vs2 index edge values at each explicit EEW encoding (8, 16, 32, 64 bit indices).
explanation: The coverpoint only tests the exception case where an unsupported EEW raises exceptions. The normative rule has two parts: (1) indexed operations use explicit EEW encoding to set index size, and (2) indexed operations use SEW/LMUL to specify data width. The coverpoint addresses neither of these functional aspects directly - it only tests the error path when EEW is unsupported.
gaps: No coverage for verifying that index element size actually matches the explicit EEW encoding in the instruction; No coverage for verifying that data width is determined by SEW/LMUL rather than the EEW field; No coverage for correct operation across different valid EEW values (8, 16, 32, 64) with varying SEW/LMUL settings

spec_text: Implementations must provide vector loads and stores with EEWs corresponding to all supported SEW settings.
coverage_desc_1: Tests the boundary between supported and unsupported EEW by verifying legal EEW executes correctly while unsupported EEW raises exceptions
coverage_desc_2: Coverpoint implicitly tests the boundary of this rule - implementations must support EEW corresponding to supported SEW settings, so EEW below SEWMIN is unsupported
explanation: The coverpoint tests the boundary between supported and unsupported EEW by checking that legal EEW executes correctly and unsupported EEW raises exceptions. This partially covers the rule by verifying that supported SEW settings have corresponding vector load/store EEWs. However, the rule requires that ALL supported SEW settings have corresponding load/store EEWs, and the coverpoint focuses on exception behavior at boundaries rather than systematically verifying that every supported SEW has a working vector load and store.
gaps: No systematic verification that vector loads exist and function correctly for every supported SEW setting; No systematic verification that vector stores exist and function correctly for every supported SEW setting; Coverage focuses on exception boundary behavior rather than positive confirmation of all required EEW support

spec_text: Vector load/store encodings for unsupported EEW widths are reserved.
coverage_desc_1: Directly tests that vector load/store encodings for unsupported EEW widths are reserved and raise illegal instruction exceptions
coverage_desc_2: Coverpoint directly tests that unsupported EEW widths (2*ELEN) in vector load/store encodings are treated as reserved and trap
coverage_desc_3: Coverpoint directly tests that vector load/store encodings with unsupported EEW widths (EEW < SEWMIN) are reserved and cause a trap
explanation: The coverpoint cp_exceptionsv_LS_stdtrapvec directly tests that vector load/store encodings for unsupported EEW widths are reserved by verifying they raise illegal instruction exceptions, which is exactly what the normative rule requires.

spec_text: The vector offset operand is treated as a vector of byte-address offsets.
coverage_desc_1: cp_vs2_edges ls variant tests vs2 offset edge values {0, random < 2*VLMAX} which are byte-address offsets, exercising the rule that vector offset operands are treated as byte-address offsets.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: If the vector offset elements are narrower than XLEN, they are zero-extended to XLEN before adding to the base effective address.  If the vector offset elements are wider than XLEN, the least-significant XLEN bits are used in the address calculation.
coverage_desc_1: This coverpoint directly tests that vector offset elements narrower than XLEN are zero-extended (not sign-extended) before adding to the base effective address, by using SEW=8/16 offsets set to all ones and verifying the unsigned interpretation is used.
coverage_desc_2: The coverpoint tests that when vector offset elements are wider than XLEN (SEW=64 on RV32), the least-significant XLEN bits are used in the address calculation, which is exactly the truncation behavior described by this rule.
coverage_desc_3: cp_vs2_edges ls variant tests edge offset values in vs2 elements which interact with XLEN-dependent zero-extension or truncation when offset element width differs from XLEN.
explanation: The zero-extension testing covers SEW=8 and SEW=16 but misses SEW=32 on RV64 (where 32-bit offsets are also narrower than XLEN=64 and must be zero-extended). The truncation coverpoint covers SEW=64 on RV32. The two halves of the rule (zero-extend when narrower, use least-significant XLEN bits when wider) are addressed, but the zero-extension case has an incomplete SEW coverage gap.
gaps: Missing cp_custom_ls_indexed_zero_extended_sew32 for RV64 where SEW=32 offsets are narrower than XLEN=64 and should be zero-extended

spec_text: If the implementation does not support the EEW of the offset elements, the instruction is reserved.
coverage_desc_1: Tests that unsupported EEW for offset elements raises illegal instruction exceptions
coverage_desc_2: Coverpoint directly tests that when the implementation does not support the EEW (because it is below SEWMIN), the instruction is treated as reserved
explanation: The coverpoint tests that unsupported EEW for offset elements raises an illegal instruction exception, which covers the behavioral outcome. However, the normative rule states the instruction is 'reserved' when EEW is unsupported, and reserved behavior is implementation-defined - it does not strictly require an illegal instruction exception. The coverpoint assumes one specific reserved behavior (trap) rather than covering the full range of what 'reserved' means. Additionally, there is no coverage verifying which specific EEW values are unsupported for the implementation under test.
gaps: No coverage for determining which EEW values are actually unsupported by the implementation; Reserved behavior is not necessarily an illegal instruction exception - the coverpoint assumes a specific reserved behavior rather than testing the general 'reserved' status

spec_text: Vector unit-stride and constant-stride memory accesses do not guarantee ordering between individual element accesses.  The vector indexed load and store memory operations have two forms, ordered and unordered.  The indexed-ordered variants preserve element ordering on memory accesses.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: For unordered instructions (mop[1:0]!=11) there is no guarantee on element access order.  If the accesses are to a strongly ordered IO region, the element accesses can be initiated in any order.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: For implementations with precise vector traps, exceptions on indexed-unordered stores must also be precise.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: The nf[2:0] field encodes the number of fields in each segment.  For regular vector loads and stores, nf=0, indicating that a single value is moved between a vector register group and memory at each element position.  Larger values in the nf field are used to access multiple contiguous fields within a segment as described below in .
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: The nf[2:0] field also encodes the number of whole vector registers to transfer for the whole vector register load/store instructions.
coverage_desc_1: The coverpoint tests whole register load/store instructions which use the nf field to encode the number of whole vector registers to transfer
coverage_desc_2: Coverpoint verifies that nf encodes the number of whole vector registers transferred, independent of LMUL
coverage_desc_3: Coverpoint exercises the nf field encoding for whole register load/store instructions by using various nf values including reserved ones.
explanation: The normative rule states that nf[2:0] encodes the number of whole vector registers to transfer for whole vector register load/store instructions. cp_custom_vwholeRegLS_vill tests whole register load/store instructions using the nf field to encode the number of registers transferred, and cp_custom_vwholeRegLS_lmul verifies that nf encodes the number of whole vector registers transferred independent of LMUL. Together these coverpoints fully test the nf encoding behavior for whole register load/store instructions.

spec_text: Vector loads and stores have an EEW encoded directly in the instruction.  The corresponding EMUL is calculated as EMUL = (EEW/SEW)*LMUL.
coverage_desc_1: Tests the EEW encoded directly in vector load/store instructions, verifying behavior for both supported and unsupported widths
coverage_desc_2: Coverpoint exercises vector load/store EEW encoding with EEW=8 for mask operations across different SEW/LMUL settings
coverage_desc_3: Tests across different EEW values encoded in segment load/store instructions to create NFIELDS * EEW violations
coverage_desc_4: Coverpoint tests vector load/store instructions with EEW encoded directly in the instruction, specifically testing unsupported EEW = 2*ELEN
coverage_desc_5: Coverpoint tests vector load/store instructions where EEW is encoded directly in the instruction, verifying behavior when that EEW is unsupported (less than SEWMIN)
explanation: The first coverpoint tests EEW encoding for supported/unsupported widths, and the second tests EEW=8 mask operations with different SEW/LMUL settings. However, the rule states EMUL = (EEW/SEW)*LMUL, and coverage gaps exist around systematically verifying the EMUL calculation across various EEW/SEW/LMUL combinations beyond just EEW=8 mask operations.
gaps: Systematic testing of EMUL = (EEW/SEW)*LMUL calculation across all valid EEW values (8, 16, 32, 64) combined with various SEW and LMUL settings; Verification of behavior when calculated EMUL is out of valid range (e.g., EMUL > 8 or EMUL < 1/8)

spec_text: Vector loads and stores have an EEW encoded directly in the instruction.  The corresponding EMUL is calculated as EMUL = (EEW/SEW)*LMUL.
coverage_desc_1: Coverpoint tests EMUL calculation for mask load/stores where EMUL = (EEW/SEW)*LMUL, but mask operations override to EMUL=1
coverage_desc_2: EEW determines EMUL via EMUL = (EEW/SEW)*LMUL, so varying EEW indirectly exercises EMUL calculation for segment instructions
coverage_desc_3: Coverpoint exercises EMUL = (EEW/SEW)*LMUL calculation for vector load/store instructions with specific EEW, SEW, and LMUL values producing EMUL=16
coverage_desc_4: The coverpoint uses vector load/store instructions where EMUL is calculated from EEW/SEW*LMUL, directly exercising the EMUL calculation for vector loads and stores.
coverage_desc_5: Coverpoint exercises the EMUL = (EEW/SEW)*LMUL calculation for vector loads/stores by choosing parameters that make the result exceed 8.
coverage_desc_6: Tests the EMUL = (EEW/SEW)*LMUL calculation for vector loads/stores where the result is < 1/8
explanation: The coverpoint only tests EMUL calculation for mask load/stores, which are a special case where EMUL is overridden to 1. The normative rule describes the general EMUL = (EEW/SEW)*LMUL calculation for all vector loads and stores, not just mask operations.
gaps: No coverage of EMUL = (EEW/SEW)*LMUL calculation for non-mask vector loads (unit-stride, strided, indexed); No coverage of EMUL = (EEW/SEW)*LMUL calculation for non-mask vector stores (unit-stride, strided, indexed); No coverage of varying EEW values (8, 16, 32, 64) with different SEW and LMUL combinations; No coverage verifying correct EMUL results across the full range of valid LMUL and SEW settings

spec_text: If the EMUL would be out of range (EMUL>8 or EMUL<1/8), the instruction encoding is reserved.
coverage_desc_1: If EMUL derived from EEW would be out of range, the encoding is reserved - related to unsupported EEW combinations raising exceptions
coverage_desc_2: Coverpoint directly tests that EMUL>8 (EMUL=16) causes the instruction encoding to be reserved, triggering a trap
coverage_desc_3: The coverpoint specifically tests that EMUL=1/16 (which is < 1/8, out of range) causes a trap, directly covering the rule that out-of-range EMUL makes the instruction encoding reserved.
coverage_desc_4: Coverpoint directly targets this rule by confirming that when EMUL>8 for a vector load/store, the instruction encoding is treated as reserved and traps.
coverage_desc_5: Directly tests that indexed load/store traps when EMUL < 1/8, which is the out-of-range EMUL reserved encoding condition specified by this rule
explanation: The coverpoint cp_exceptionsv_LS_stdtrapvec covers the case where EMUL derived from EEW is out of range and raises an exception (illegal instruction trap). However, the normative rule states the encoding is 'reserved', which in RISC-V can mean either raising an illegal instruction exception OR implementation-defined behavior depending on context. The coverpoint only checks the exception/trap path for unsupported EEW combinations, but does not explicitly verify both EMUL>8 and EMUL<1/8 boundary conditions independently.
gaps: No explicit coverage of EMUL>8 boundary condition separate from EMUL<1/8; No coverage verifying behavior for non-exception reserved encoding handling (if implementation does not trap on reserved encodings)

spec_text: The vector register groups must have legal register specifiers for the selected EMUL, otherwise the instruction encoding is reserved.
coverage_desc_1: The emul2, emul4, and emul8 variants for whole register stores (vs2r.v, vs4r.v, vs8r.v) ensure vs3 has legal aligned register specifiers for the selected EMUL.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: Vector unit-stride and constant-stride use the EEW/EMUL encoded in the instruction for the data values, while vector indexed loads and stores use the EEW/EMUL encoded in the instruction for the index values and the SEW/LMUL encoded in vtype for the data values.
coverage_desc_1: Relies on the distinction that indexed loads/stores use SEW/LMUL for data and EEW/EMUL from instruction for indices, which is why the constraint only applies to data group
coverage_desc_2: Coverpoint directly tests the index EMUL calculation for indexed loads/stores by using EEW/SEW/LMUL combinations that produce EMUL>8.
coverage_desc_3: Tests indexed load/store EMUL calculation for index values where the resulting EMUL is out of range (< 1/8)
coverage_desc_4: cp_vs2_edges across different EEW-encoded indexed instructions exercises the EMUL=(EEW/SEW)*LMUL calculation for the index vector register group in vs2.
explanation: The coverpoints test the data side (SEW/LMUL) of indexed loads/stores, but the rule also specifies that EEW/EMUL from the instruction is used for index values in indexed operations, and that unit-stride/constant-stride use EEW/EMUL for data values. The index EEW/EMUL aspect and the unit-stride/constant-stride behavior are not covered.
gaps: No coverpoint testing that indexed loads/stores use EEW/EMUL encoded in the instruction for index values; No coverpoint testing that unit-stride and constant-stride operations use EEW/EMUL encoded in the instruction for data values

spec_text: The mew bit (inst[28]) when set is expected to be used to encode expanded memory sizes of 128 bits and above, but these encodings are currently reserved.
coverage_desc_1: The mew bit encodings for 128-bit+ memory sizes are reserved - tests that these unsupported EEW encodings raise exceptions
coverage_desc_2: EEW = 2*ELEN (e.g., 128-bit when ELEN=64) requires setting the mew bit to encode expanded memory sizes of 128 bits and above, which is reserved
coverage_desc_3: Directly tests that vector load/store instructions with mew bit (inst[28]) set are treated as reserved encodings and cause a trap
explanation: The normative rule states that mew=1 encodings are reserved (for 128-bit+ memory sizes). The coverpoint cp_exceptionsv_LS_stdtrapvec tests that these reserved EEW encodings raise exceptions, which is the expected behavior for reserved encodings. This fully covers the rule since the only testable aspect of a reserved encoding is that it triggers an illegal instruction exception.

spec_text: Additional unit-stride mask load and store instructions are provided to transfer mask values to/from memory.  These operate similarly to unmasked byte loads or stores (EEW=8), except that the effective vector length is evl=ceil(vl/8) (i.e. EMUL=1), and the destination register is always written with a tail-agnostic policy.
coverage_desc_1: Coverpoint directly tests mask load/store instructions which operate with EEW=8 and EMUL=1, verifying they execute correctly regardless of vtype settings
explanation: The coverpoint tests mask load/store with EEW=8 and EMUL=1 regardless of vtype settings, which covers the basic operation and the EMUL=1 aspect. However, several specific aspects of the normative rule are not covered.
gaps: No coverpoint verifying that effective vector length is evl=ceil(vl/8) rather than vl; No coverpoint verifying tail-agnostic policy is always applied to the destination register regardless of vta setting; No coverpoint verifying the instructions operate similarly to unmasked byte loads/stores (i.e., no masking applied)

spec_text: Negative and zero strides are supported.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: Negative and zero strides are supported.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: Element accesses within a constant-stride instruction are unordered with respect to each other.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: When rs2=x0, then an implementation is allowed, but not required, to perform fewer memory operations than the number of active elements, and may perform different numbers of memory operations across different dynamic executions of the same static instruction.
coverage_desc_1: cp_rs2 includes rs2=x0 (register 0) among its 32 register values, partially covering the special-case rule about rs2=x0 allowing fewer memory operations.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: The unit-stride fault-only-first load instructions are used to vectorize loops with data-dependent exit conditions ("while" loops). These instructions execute as a regular load except that they will only take a trap caused by a synchronous exception on element 0.
coverage_desc_1: Tests that a synchronous exception on element 0 causes a trap, confirming fault-only-first instructions take traps on element 0.
coverage_desc_2: Coverpoint uses unit-stride fault-only-first loads and verifies they only trap on element 0 exceptions, not on later elements
explanation: The normative rule states that fault-only-first loads execute as regular loads except they only trap on synchronous exceptions on element 0. cp_exceptionsv_ffLS_first_elm_trap directly tests that element 0 exceptions cause traps, and cp_custom_ffLS_update_vl verifies that exceptions on later elements do not cause traps. Together these two coverpoints cover both aspects of the rule: trapping on element 0 and not trapping on non-zero elements.

spec_text: Load instructions may overwrite active destination vector register group elements past the element index at which the trap is reported.
coverage_desc_1: When the address fault trap occurs on a vector load, the behavior of destination elements past the trap element index is exercised, partially covering this rule.
explanation: The coverpoint only exercises address fault traps on vector loads, but the normative rule applies to all trap types that can occur during vector loads (e.g., page faults, access faults, misaligned exceptions). Additionally, the coverpoint only partially covers the behavior of destination elements past the trap element index - it does not explicitly verify that elements may be overwritten (i.e., that the implementation is permitted to modify those elements).
gaps: Only address faults are covered; other trap types (page faults, access faults) during vector loads are not exercised; No explicit verification that destination elements past the trap index are actually overwritten or may contain modified values; No coverage of different vector load types (unit-stride, strided, indexed) which may have different overwrite behaviors past the trap element

spec_text: Similarly, fault-only-first load instructions may update active destination elements past the element that causes trimming of the vector length (but not past the original vector length).  The values of these spurious updates do not have to correspond to the values in memory at the addressed memory locations.  Non-idempotent memory locations can only be accessed when it is known the corresponding element load operation will not be restarted due to a trap or vector-length trimming.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: Even when an exception is not raised, implementations are permitted to process fewer than vl elements and reduce vl accordingly, but if vstart=0 and vl>0, then at least one element must be processed.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: When the fault-only-first instruction takes a trap due to an interrupt, implementations should not reduce vl and should instead set a vstart value.
explanation: No coverpoints paired to this rule

spec_text: The three-bit nf field in the vector instruction encoding is an unsigned integer that contains one less than the number of fields per segment, NFIELDS. ||| Each field will be held in successively numbered vector register groups.  When EMUL>1, each field will occupy a vector register group held in multiple successively numbered vector registers, and the vector register group for each field must follow the usual vector register alignment constraints (e.g., when EMUL=2 and NFIELDS=4, each field’s vector register group must start at an even vector register, but does not have to start at a multiple of 8 vector register number).
coverage_desc_1: Tests multiple NFIELDS values (2, 4, 8) to exercise the segment field count in combination with LMUL at the constraint boundary
coverage_desc_2: Exercises various NFIELDS values (encoded in nf field) in combination with EEW to trigger the reservation condition
coverage_desc_3: Tests with specific NFIELDS values and EMUL>1 where fields occupy successively numbered vector register groups that overflow past v31
coverage_desc_4: The lte30-lte24 variants for vsseg2-vsseg8 store instructions ensure successively numbered vector register groups for each field stay within bounds, partially covering the NFIELDS segment register allocation rule.
explanation: The coverpoints test NFIELDS values of 2, 4, and 8 in combination with LMUL, which exercises segment field counts and register group alignment. However, the rule specifies NFIELDS is encoded as a 3-bit field (nf) representing 1-8 fields. The coverpoints only test 2, 4, and 8, missing NFIELDS values of 1, 3, 5, 6, and 7. Additionally, the rule states each field occupies successively numbered vector register groups with alignment constraints when EMUL>1, but coverage of the specific alignment requirement (e.g., EMUL=2 fields starting at even registers but not necessarily multiples of 8) is not explicitly confirmed for all EMUL/NFIELDS combinations.
gaps: Missing NFIELDS values 1, 3, 5, 6, and 7 (only 2, 4, 8 are tested); Explicit verification that fields are held in successively numbered vector register groups is not confirmed; The specific alignment example (EMUL=2, NFIELDS=4, fields starting at even but not necessarily multiple-of-8 registers) may not be directly tested

spec_text: The EMUL setting must be such that EMUL * NFIELDS ≤ 8, otherwise the instruction encoding is reserved.

The normative rule states EMUL*NFIELDS ≤ 8, which includes both valid cases (EMUL*NFIELDS ≤ 8) and reserved/invalid cases (EMUL*NFIELDS > 8). The coverpoints do not test that encodings where EMUL*NFIELDS > 8 are treated as reserved.

spec_text: The instructions operate with an effective vector length, evl=NFIELDS*VLEN/EEW, regardless of current settings in vtype and vl.  The usual property that no elements are written if vstart ≥ vl does not apply to these instructions. Similarly, the property that the instructions are reserved if vstart exceeds the largest element index for the current vtype setting does not apply. Instead, the instructions are reserved if vstart ≥ evl.
coverage_desc_1: Whole register loads/stores operate with an effective vector length independent of vtype and vl settings, which is why they are not affected by vill - this coverpoint verifies that behavior
coverage_desc_2: Coverpoint confirms whole register load/stores operate with evl=NFIELDS*VLEN/EEW regardless of current vtype and vl settings, by varying LMUL and observing no effect
coverage_desc_3: The coverpoint directly tests that vstart is compared against evl (NFIELDS*VLEN/EEW) rather than vl for whole register load/store instructions, which is the core behavior specified by this rule.
explanation: The coverpoints test that whole register load/stores are independent of vill, LMUL, and that vstart is compared against evl rather than vl. However, the rule also states that the usual property 'no elements are written if vstart >= vl' does NOT apply, and that the instructions are reserved if vstart >= evl. The coverpoints test vstart vs evl comparison but do not explicitly verify that elements ARE still written when vstart >= vl but vstart < evl, nor do they test the reserved behavior when vstart >= evl.
gaps: No coverpoint verifies that elements are written when vstart >= vl but vstart < evl (proving the usual vstart >= vl property does not apply); No coverpoint verifies reserved behavior when vstart >= evl

spec_text: This is a unary vector-vector instruction that returns an estimate of 1/sqrt(x) accurate to 7 bits. ||| For the non-exceptional cases, the low bit of the exponent and the six high bits of significand (after the leading one) are concatenated and used to address the following table. The output of the table becomes the seven high bits of the result significand (after the leading one); the remainder of the result significand is zero. Subnormal inputs are normalized and the exponent adjusted appropriately before the lookup. The output exponent is chosen to make the result approximate the reciprocal of the square root of the argument. ||| More precisely, the result is computed as follows. Let the normalized input exponent be equal to the input exponent if the input is normal, or 0 minus the number of leading zeros in the significand otherwise. If the input is subnormal, the normalized input significand is given by shifting the input significand left by 1 minus the normalized input exponent, discarding the leading 1 bit. The output exponent equals floor((3*B - 1 - the normalized input exponent) / 2), where B is the exponent bias. The output sign equals the input sign.
coverage_desc_1: The coverpoint uses vfrsqrt7.v as its test instruction, exercising the reciprocal square root estimate operation with a specific input (vs2=0).
coverage_desc_2: Coverpoint tests edge cases from the vfrsqrt7 behavior table (all classes of FP inputs), partially covering the instruction's specified operation and expected results.
coverage_desc_3: The coverpoint directly tests the reciprocal square-root estimate lookup table by exercising all possible 7-bit inputs (low exponent bit + 6 high significand bits) and verifying the 7-bit output significand matches the spec table.
explanation: The lookup table itself is well covered by cp_custom_FpRecSqrtEst_edges (all 128 table entries), and edge-case input classes are covered by cp_custom_FpRecSqrtEst_flag_edges. However, several aspects of the normative rule lack dedicated coverage.
gaps: Subnormal input normalization: the spec describes normalizing subnormal inputs by computing a normalized exponent (0 minus leading zeros) and shifting the significand, but no coverpoint specifically verifies this normalization process produces correct table lookup inputs; Output exponent computation: the formula floor((3*B - 1 - normalized_input_exponent) / 2) is not explicitly verified by any coverpoint; Output sign equals input sign: no coverpoint specifically checks that the result sign is preserved from the input; Remainder of result significand is zero: no coverpoint verifies that bits below the 7 high significand bits are zeroed

spec_text: This is a unary vector-vector instruction that returns an estimate of 1/x accurate to 7 bits. ||| For the non-exceptional cases, the seven high bits of significand (after the leading one) are used to address the following table. The output of the table becomes the seven high bits of the result significand (after the leading one); the remainder of the result significand is zero. Subnormal inputs are normalized and the exponent adjusted appropriately before the lookup. The output exponent is chosen to make the result approximate the reciprocal of the argument, and subnormal outputs are denormalized accordingly. ||| More precisely, the result is computed as follows. Let the normalized input exponent be equal to the input exponent if the input is normal, or 0 minus the number of leading zeros in the significand otherwise. The normalized output exponent equals (2*B - 1 - the normalized input exponent). If the normalized output exponent is outside the range [-1, 2*B], the result corresponds to one of the exceptional cases in the table above. ||| If the input is subnormal, the normalized input significand is given by shifting the input significand left by 1 minus the normalized input exponent, discarding the leading 1 bit. Otherwise, the normalized input significand equals the input significand. The following table gives the seven MSBs of the normalized output significand as a function of the seven MSBs of the normalized input significand; the other bits of the normalized output significand are zero. ||| If the normalized output exponent is 0 or -1, the result is subnormal: the output exponent is 0, and the output significand is given by concatenating a 1 bit to the left of the normalized output significand, then shifting that quantity right by 1 minus the normalized output exponent. Otherwise, the output exponent equals the normalized output exponent, and the output significand equals the normalized output significand. The output sign equals the input sign.
coverage_desc_1: Coverpoint tests edge cases from the vfrec7 behavior table including exceptional cases and flag setting, covering the reciprocal estimate operation specification
coverage_desc_2: The coverpoint tests all 128 possible 7-bit input significand values against the spec's lookup table, directly verifying the table-based reciprocal estimate computation that is the core of this rule.
explanation: The two coverpoints cover the lookup table (all 128 input significand entries) and the exceptional cases with flag setting. However, several aspects of the normative rule are not explicitly covered.
gaps: Subnormal input normalization: the rule specifies how subnormal inputs have their significand shifted and exponent adjusted before lookup, but no coverpoint specifically tests this normalization process; Normalized output exponent computation: the formula (2*B - 1 - normalized_input_exponent) is not explicitly verified across different exponent values and floating-point formats; Subnormal output denormalization: the rule describes specific right-shifting behavior when normalized output exponent is 0 or -1, which is not explicitly covered as a separate concern; Sign preservation: the rule states output sign equals input sign, which is not explicitly listed as a tested property; Multiple floating-point format coverage: the rule applies across SEW=16/32/64 with different bias values (B), and coverage of format-specific exponent handling is not evident

spec_text: The implementation must produce a result equivalent to a reduction tree composed of binary operator nodes, with the inputs being elements from the source vector register group (vs2) and the source scalar value (vs1[0]).  Each operator in the tree accepts two inputs and produces one result. Each operator first computes an exact sum as a RISC-V scalar floating-point addition with infinite exponent range and precision, then converts this exact sum to a floating-point format with range and precision each at least as great as the element floating-point format indicated by SEW, rounding using the currently active floating-point dynamic rounding mode and raising exception flags as necessary. A different floating-point range and precision may be chosen for the result of each operator. A node where one input is derived only from elements masked-off or beyond the active vector length may either treat that input as the additive identity of the appropriate EEW or simply copy the other input to its output. The rounded result from the root node in the tree is converted (rounded again, using the dynamic rounding mode) to the standard floating-point format indicated by SEW.

spec_text: The vtype LMUL setting can be used to indicate or calculate the effective length multiplier (EMUL) for one or more operands.  Element group instructions tend to exhibit a much wider range of relationships between various operand EEW/EMUL values.  For example, an instruction might take a vector of length N of 4-element groups with EEW=8b and reduce each group to produce a vector length N of 1-element groups with EEW=32b. In this case, the input and output EMUL values are equal even though the EEW settings differ by a factor of 4.
